newsitem.title: KENYA: French expert has plan to save refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: French expert has plan to save refugees in Zaire.

text.p: The French army should intervene quickly in eastern Zaire to save more than a million Hutu refugees but only after getting Rwanda's blessing, a French expert proposed on Saturday.

Gerard Prunier, an academic who advised France's broadly successful "Operation Turquoise" in the same region in 1994, said hundreds of thousands of refugees faced death from cholera unless safe passage west deeper into Zaire is rapidly organised.
"If there is no decision by Monday it will be too late," Prunier told Reuters by telephone from Paris. His plan was presented to French government officials on Friday.
"I am suggesting a unilateral French operation because we have the military capacity in Africa," Prunier said.
"We may have to forget about the rest of Europe and the U.N. because it will take too long. But if others want to get involved, that's fine."
A lightning offensive by Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire has thrown Zaire's army into disarray and left more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees at high risk.
The last of the foreign aid workers who cared for them all fled into Rwanda on Saturday and about 400,000 refugees are now crammed into Mugunga camp on the shores of Lake Kivu near Goma.

About 50,000 Rwandan refugees died from cholera in a matter of days in July 1994 when they fled their homeland fearing reprisal for the genocide against the Tutsi minority in which many took part. "Operation Turquoise" helped them reach Zaire.
Aid workers say cholera will spread fast this time, particularly in Mugunga, where refugees drink unsafe water from the lake. At least 600,000 more refugees are roaming east Zaire.
Their plight has led to international calls for action, but Western countries are divided. There are no declared volunteers to head the operation, although Italy said it was ready to help.
The influential French daily Le Monde reported on Saturday the European Union was considering opening militarily protected "humanitarian corridors" in Zaire to help the refugees.
It wrote from Brussels that such an operation might involve French, Belgian and South African troops.
Le Monde said France told its partners it would not intervene militarily unless it was mandated to do so, preferably by the Organisation of African Unity.
Tutsi army chiefs in Rwanda, led by Vice-President Paul Kagame, would suspect any French involvement because Paris supported the former Hutu government, diplomats say.
Prunier's plan takes those Tutsi concerns into account.
"Clearly Kagame would need to be told, 'OK, you've won the war in Kivu (eastern Zaire) but let's have a buffer zone and get the refugees to safety,'" he said.
U.S. backing for the plan was needed to assure Tutsis France had no military agenda to shore up Zaire's army, he said.
The benefit for Rwanda is that fighters among the Hutus would be too far away to continue mounting the cross-border incursions of the past two years.
The main opposition will come from Zaire which said on Friday the refugees must go back to Rwanda.
"But the Zaireans will not be able to stop the mass of Hutus moving west if they decide to go," Prunier said.
Prunier said his idea was to get safe passage for the Hutus to walk about 100 km (60 miles) west of their current sites.
In an area with no motorable roads, French troops using helicopters based in the Central African Republic could pre-position food, water and medicine to sustain the refugees during the trek.
Prunier, like other experts, said the Hutus who include the ex-Rwandan army and the Interahamwe militiamen responsible for the genocide will refuse to go back to Rwanda.
